<reason>PRO wins because CON's opening handed it the debate: proposing a mandatory injury surcharge administered by the company, then adding verified ID, app-deducted fines, suspensions, and penalties for missed slowdowns. PRO relentlessly and accurately framed each as a new legal duty on the company triggered by rider-on-pedestrian injuries, which is what "more legal responsibility" plainly means. CON's defense depended on narrowing the motion to fault-attribution to the victim, but PRO's point that a fund paying the pedestrian directly is a duty to her, plus catching CON's drift from "no wrongful act" to "the company's own breach," left CON defending a label. CON scored real hits — the GPS-margin dilemma showed PRO's presumption fires only in easy cases, and PRO's pay-first-recover scheme mirrors CON's collection-agent model — and CON's "hand on the throttle vs. hand on the server" was memorable. But those points establish overlap, not that the company should bear no more responsibility than today. PRO answered both pressure questions honestly with A1:/A2: structure; PRO's two clipped turns are a modest execution cost that keeps the margin competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 1 ([A2.1]-[A2.2]) turning CON's own surcharge proposal into a concession of the motion, reinforced in [A4.6] and [A5.3] where PRO showed CON had migrated from "committed no wrongful act" to "the company's own breach." CON's strongest counter was [B4.4]-[B4.5], showing PRO's presumption only triggers in easy cases and its pay-first scheme is CON's collection model renamed, but that narrowed rather than reversed the concession.</best_rebuttal>
